newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Islamic leaders watch Pakistan's jubilee parade.
newsitem.headline: Islamic leaders watch Pakistan's jubilee parade.

text.p: Islamic leaders watched a military parade through Islamabad on Sunday before attending a special one-day summit conference to greet Pakistan in its golden jubilee year.
President Farooq Leghari, who arrived at the reviewing stand in a horse-drawn buggy flanked by cavalry, inspected an honour guard before air force jets screamed overhead in formation.
"It is our great honour that Moslem leaders from all over the world are participating in the celebrations of our 50 years of independence," Leghari said in a speech.
"I pray to God the Moslem Ummah (nation) remains united as shown by the presence of the heads of states here," he added.
Leghari said March 23 marked a milestone in Pakistan's history, commemorating a 1940 declaration setting out the goal of creating a homeland for Moslems in the sub-continent.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, Turkish President Suleyman Demirel and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat were the most prominent leaders watching the parade.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Abdullah and Bangladesh's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, the only woman leader to attend, were also there, but Arab heads of state mostly stayed away.

The summit of the 54-nation Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) is intended to underline the Moslem world's solidarity with Pakistan, which emerged as an independent country in 1947 from the partition of British-ruled India.

It has a single-point agenda on "preparing the Islamic world for the 21st century". The summit declaration will refer to problems facing the Moslem world in political, economic and other fields and suggest ways to overcome them, Pakistani spokesman Inamul Haq told a news conference on Saturday.

These problems include what he called "cultural aggresssion" directed against Islamic countries in the Western media. The declaration would also highlight the Palestinian issue and Pakistan's dispute with arch-rival India over Kashmir, he said.
With Arab kings and potentates staying at home, the summit was expected to prove a largely ceremonial affair.
Morocco's King Hassan, the current chairman of the 27-year-old OIC, did not come, but sent a message to the summit.

Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak, citing Middle East tension, sent his regrets, as did Syria's President Hafez al-Assad, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, King Hussein of Jordan and the heads of state of Algeria, Tunisia and Libya.
Afghanistan's seat at the conference remained empty, the OIC having decided earlier not to recognise any of the warring Afghan factions as the legitimate government.
But representatives of the Taleban Islamic movement, which controls Kabul and more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, and some other Afghans, attended the summit as guests.
